correctness.rationale: Every nonzero complex input X is reduced to its Frobenius square F and its determinant, and the weak target to the same F and modified determinant. The AM–GM estimate yields |alpha|+|beta|<=1. Solving a two-focus ellipse gives the exact maximal modified determinant at fixed original determinant, with radial maximum equal to u cos(theta/2)+sin(theta/2)sqrt(1-u²) for u<=cos(theta/2), and one otherwise. The resulting squared ratio is increasing before and decreasing after the switch; an explicit balanced matrix gives equality. The separate largest singular value is <=||X||_1. Endpoint theta=0 and theta=pi, phase gauge, and all quantifiers are handled. 400000 seeded complex samples across eight phases and eight analytic extremizers agreed; the proof does not rely on sampling.

originality.rationale: The 2026 full primary paper specifies the weak target and proves a column-width comparison within factor two, not the sharp 2-by-2 phase-dependent value. Older inspected Davidson–Donsig concerns the strong bounded-operator Schur multiplier norm; Banks–Harcharras treats idempotents on S_p with p>1, neither implying the weak trace-class formula. Database searches for the cross-ratio phase, sharp secant-quarter formula, Hadamard and Lorentz aliases returned no equivalent result. A related Schatten-four idempotent exact gap has a different symbol and target. Residual risk: an older unindexed 2-by-2 weak Lorentz endpoint computation may be equivalent.

value.rationale: This is the complete gauge-invariant sharp weak trace endpoint norm for every complex unimodular two-by-two Schur symbol, the first nontrivial complex phase family for a recently motivated endpoint criterion. The optimal weak-norm distortion varies quadratically in phase near rank-one symbols while a strong trace-norm rank-one witness shows linear phase distortion; the analysis identifies the ellipse transition generating this difference. It is a motivated, exact complete classification of a natural finite family rather than an arbitrary numeric slice. No higher-dimensional theorem is asserted.
